# The radiative transfer equation {#sec-rte}

Consider a small volume of water. The number of photons inside it changes
when photons cross its boundary, are created inside it, or are absorbed.
Scattering does not change the total number of photons, but it moves them
between directions. If the observable of interest is not just the light
density but the signal of a directional receiver, that exchange between
directions has to be tracked explicitly.

Fix one wavelength; polarization and wavelength change on scattering are not
treated here. Between interactions a photon travels in a straight line at
constant group speed $v$. The optical properties are given and are not
modified by the light itself. What is modeled is the mean photon
distribution, not an electromagnetic amplitude or one random realization.
This kinetic description applies at scales where intensities can be added
and coherent interference is negligible [see e.g. Arridge & Schotland,
*Inverse Problems* **25**, 123010 (2009)].

## What is transported {#sec-intensity}

Let $\mathbf x$ be position, $t$ time, and $\mathbf s$ the unit direction of
travel. Direction has two independent coordinates, usually polar and
azimuthal angle. On the sphere of directions,
$$
\mathrm d\Omega=\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi,
\qquad \int_{S^2}\mathrm d\Omega=4\pi.
$$

Define the angular photon-number density $f$ by
$$
\mathrm dN=f(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t)\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega,
$$ {#eq-angular-density}
the expected number of photons in a spatial volume $\mathrm d^3x$ whose
direction lies in the solid-angle element $\mathrm d\Omega$. It is more
convenient to work with the angular intensity
$$
I(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t)=v\,f(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t).
$$ {#eq-intensity-definition}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why the extra factor of v"}
In time $\mathrm dt$, the photons that cross an area element $\mathrm dA$
perpendicular to $\mathbf s$ come from a cylinder of volume
$v\,\mathrm dt\,\mathrm dA$, so
$$
\mathrm dN_{\mathrm{cross}}=I\,\mathrm dA\,\mathrm dt\,\mathrm d\Omega.
$$
For a surface with normal $\mathbf n$ and $\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf n>0$, its
projected area contributes an extra factor $\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf n$. The
signed flux through an oriented surface is $I\,\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf n$; its
sign distinguishes an outgoing from an incoming crossing.

With length in metres and time in nanoseconds,
$$
[f]=\frac{\text{photon}}{\mathrm m^3\,\mathrm{sr}},\qquad
[I]=\frac{\text{photon}}{\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm{ns}\,\mathrm{sr}}.
$$
The photon count can be treated as dimensionless, but keeping the word
"photon" in the units is a useful check on every normalization below. A
spectral intensity $I_\lambda$ carries an additional inverse wavelength
unit; every equation in this chapter then applies wavelength by wavelength,
as long as scattering is elastic.
:::

## Streaming across a volume boundary {#sec-streaming}

Take a fixed volume $W$ with outward normal $\mathbf n$. For a narrow
direction element $\mathrm d\Omega$, the number of photons inside it is
$$
N_{W,\mathrm d\Omega}(t)=\mathrm d\Omega\int_W\frac{I}{v}\,\mathrm d^3x,
$$
and the signed outward flux through the boundary is
$$
\mathrm d\Omega\oint_{\partial W}I\,\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm dA,
$$
which already contains the incoming contribution with a negative sign. For
photons that only stream freely, with no interaction, the balance reads
$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_W\frac{I}{v}\,\mathrm d^3x
=-\oint_{\partial W}I\,\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm dA.
$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="From the surface integral to the streaming term"}
By the divergence theorem the surface integral becomes a volume integral;
at fixed direction $\mathbf s$,
$$
\int_W\left(\frac1v\frac{\partial I}{\partial t}
+\mathbf s\cdot\nabla I\right)\mathrm d^3x=0.
$$
$W$ is arbitrary, so without interactions
$$
\left(\frac1v\partial_t+\mathbf s\cdot\nabla\right)I=0.
$$ {#eq-free-streaming}
The two terms are not two separate mechanisms: together they say that the
distribution is unchanged along a ray. The first term is the change seen at
a fixed point; the second is the imbalance between what leaves and what
enters that point.
:::

## Losses out of a chosen direction {#sec-losses}

On a short path $\mathrm d\ell$,
$$
\Pr(\text{absorption on }\mathrm d\ell)=\mu_a\,\mathrm d\ell+o(\mathrm d\ell),
\qquad
\Pr(\text{scattering on }\mathrm d\ell)=\mu_s\,\mathrm d\ell+o(\mathrm d\ell),
$$
with $\mu_a,\mu_s$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. In a homogeneous medium
$\ell_a=1/\mu_a$ and $\ell_s=1/\mu_s$ are the absorption and scattering
lengths treated as separate processes; the mean free path to the first
interaction of either kind is $1/(\mu_a+\mu_s)$.

In time $\mathrm dt$ a photon covers $v\,\mathrm dt$, so out of the phase
volume $\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega$ absorption removes, on average,
$$
\mathrm dN_a=\mu_a\,v f\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega\,\mathrm dt
=\mu_a I\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Scattering removes photons from the chosen direction with the same
structure, $\mu_s I$. The combined loss term in the equation for $I$ is
$$
-\mu_t I,\qquad \mu_t=\mu_a+\mu_s.
$$
An absorbed photon leaves the field being modeled. A scattered photon does
not disappear; the next section puts it back, in a new direction. For an
ordinary continuous phase function the probability of scattering into
exactly the original direction is zero; landing in a finite angular bin is
correctly handled by the gain term below.

## Gain from scattering into a chosen direction {#sec-scattering-gain}

Let $p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')$ be the conditional probability density of the
new direction $\mathbf s$ given the old direction $\mathbf s'$ — first
argument outgoing, second incoming — normalized on the outgoing direction:
$$
p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')\ge0,\qquad
\int_{S^2}p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')\,\mathrm d\Omega=1
\quad\text{for every }\mathbf s'.
$$ {#eq-phase-normalization}
Out of the incoming direction element $\mathrm d\Omega'$,
$\mu_s I(\mathbf s')\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega'$ photons scatter per
unit time; a fraction $p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')\mathrm d\Omega$ of them lands
in the outgoing direction under consideration. Summing over incoming
directions gives the gain term
$$
\mu_s\int_{S^2}p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')
I(\mathbf x,\mathbf s',t)\,\mathrm d\Omega'.
$$ {#eq-scattering-gain}
Scattering changes direction locally: position and time are the same on
both sides of this integral. Spatial displacement between collisions is
already carried by the streaming term $\mathbf s\cdot\nabla I$.

Isotropic scattering corresponds to $p=1/(4\pi)$: it makes the direction
**after** a collision uniform on the sphere. It does not follow that the
full field $I(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t)$ is isotropic — a directed source,
boundaries, or unequal path lengths to the source can all keep an angular
structure in $I$ even when every individual scattering event forgets
direction completely.

## Source and the complete balance {#sec-final-balance}

Let
$$
q(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t)\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega\,\mathrm dt
$$
be the mean number of photons created in the given volume, direction, and
time interval, so $[q]=\text{photon}/(\mathrm m^3\,\mathrm{ns}\,\mathrm{sr})$.
For isotropic emission with total directional rate $q_0$, $q=q_0/(4\pi)$.

Collecting every term,
$$
\boxed{
\frac1v\frac{\partial I}{\partial t}
+\mathbf s\cdot\nabla I
=-\mu_a I-\mu_s I
+\mu_s\int_{S^2}p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')I(\mathbf s')\,\mathrm d\Omega'
+q.
}
$$ {#eq-rte-balance}
Every term has units $\text{photon}/(\mathrm m^3\,\mathrm{ns}\,\mathrm{sr})$;
in particular, $q$ carries no separate factor of $v$, since it is already
defined as a volumetric creation rate. Writing the direction-changing
operator as
$$
(\mathcal KI)(\mathbf s)=\int_{S^2}p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')I(\mathbf s')\,\mathrm d\Omega',
$$
the balance condenses to
$$
\boxed{\left(\frac1v\partial_t+\mathbf s\cdot\nabla+\mu_t-\mu_s\mathcal K\right)I=q.}
$$ {#eq-rte}
This is the equation LightHit solves; @sec-point-source specializes it to a
point source and a point detector in an infinite homogeneous medium and
puts it in the exact form used by the code, $(D-V)h=1$ after a Fourier and
adjoint transform.

The same equation follows directly along a short ray segment:
$$
I(\mathbf x+\mathbf s\,\mathrm d\ell,\mathbf s,t+\mathrm d\ell/v)
-I(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t)
=\bigl[-\mu_tI+\mu_s\mathcal KI+q\bigr]\mathrm d\ell+o(\mathrm d\ell).
$$
The left side is the change in intensity moving with the photons; the right
side is loss, gain from other directions, and creation on that same
segment. Expanding the left side to first order returns @eq-rte.

## Check: scattering conserves photon number {#sec-number-conservation}

Define
$$
\phi(\mathbf x,t)=\int I\,\mathrm d\Omega,\qquad
n_\gamma(\mathbf x,t)=\frac{\phi}{v},\qquad
\mathbf J(\mathbf x,t)=\int\mathbf sI\,\mathrm d\Omega,
\qquad q_0=\int q\,\mathrm d\Omega,
$$ {#eq-moments-def}
the photon-number density $n_\gamma$, the scalar flux $\phi$, and the flux
vector $\mathbf J$ through an oriented surface — $\phi$ and $\mathbf J$ are
not interchangeable: in an isotropic field $\mathbf J=0$ even though $\phi$
is positive and a detector still registers photons from every side.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Integrating the balance over direction"}
Integrate @eq-rte-balance over the outgoing direction. By the phase-function
normalization @eq-phase-normalization,
$$
\int\mathrm d\Omega\int\mathrm d\Omega'\,
p(\mathbf s,\mathbf s')I(\mathbf s')=\int I(\mathbf s')\,\mathrm d\Omega',
$$
so the scattering loss and gain terms cancel exactly, leaving
$$
\boxed{\partial_tn_\gamma+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J
=-v\mu_an_\gamma+q_0.}
$$ {#eq-number-balance}
:::

@eq-number-balance is a local photon-number conservation law with
absorption and a source. It is worth checking both in a closed-form result
and in code: a non-canceling $\mu_s$ term in the full angular integral
usually points to a phase-function normalization or quadrature-weight bug.

## What else has to be specified {#sec-conditions}

One differential equation is not enough. An initial distribution
$I(\mathbf x,\mathbf s,t_0)$ is needed, and, if there is a boundary, the
intensity on incoming directions $\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf n<0$ there; the
solution then determines the outgoing intensity. A reflecting boundary
couples incoming and outgoing directions by an additional law — a different
boundary-value problem from the one treated here.

Throughout this book the medium is infinite, homogeneous, and stationary.
Before the source switches on there are no photons — the causal solution is
selected. Early on the optical coefficients could depend on position while
the ray geometry stays straight, but the independence of the spectral
problem across different $\mathbf k$, used from @sec-point-source onward,
does require a homogeneous medium.

The scalar RTE ignores polarization correlations and interference.
Inelastic scattering couples different wavelengths. A spatially varying
refractive index bends rays and requires changing the free-streaming
operator. None of these should be assumed already included in @eq-rte
merely because it is called the radiative transfer equation.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

Why does the equation for $I$ carry a $1/v$ in front of the time
derivative while the equation for $f$ does not? Derive both forms starting
from the same definition of photon number.

Show that in a homogeneous infinite medium, once a pulsed source has
finished, the total number of unabsorbed photons obeys
$\mathrm dN/\mathrm dt=-v\mu_aN$, given no flux at spatial infinity. Why
does $\mu_s$ not appear in that answer?

Consider a field with $I$ the same in every direction. Compute $\phi$,
$\mathbf J$, and the one-sided flux through a small area. Confirm that a
vanishing $\mathbf J$ does not mean the area sees no crossings.
